title.en: Papa Legba: Keeper of the Crossroads in Fon and Afro-Atlantic Vodou
title.zh: 雷格巴老爹：豐族與非裔大西洋巫毒中的十字路口守門神

region.en: Dahomey (Benin) and Haiti (diaspora; symbolic pin at Port-au-Prince)
region.zh: 達荷美（貝寧）與海地（離散地；象徵性定位於太子港）

texts.period: Fon narratives recorded 1931 fieldwork (Herskovits, published 1938); Haitian Vodou attested from 18th c. onwards; recording traditions (Verrettes? plaine du Nord) 20th c.

source.work: Legba narratives recorded by Melville J. Herskovits, Dahomey: An Ancient West African Kingdom (New York, 1938); Alfred Metraux, Voodoo in Haiti (Paris 1958/New York 1959); Karen McCarthy Brown, Mama Lola: A Vodou Priestess in Brooklyn (Berkeley, 1991)

texts.license: Paraphrase summaries only; underlying oral/liturgical texts are living tradition and are not reproduced verbatim

summary.en: Legba, the old man with the staff, guards every gate, road, and crossroads: the lwa cannot be reached without his key, the messages of the living cannot pass without his word; tricked by his own cleverness in Dahomey, enthroned as first-served in Haiti — the divine gatekeeper whose opening ritual (priye Legba) begins every Vodou ceremony.
summary.zh: 雷格巴拄杖老人，守一切門、路與十字路口：無其鑰則羅亞不至，無其言則生者之訊不通；在達荷美因巧智受騙，在海地為首奉之神——每場巫毒儀式以『雷格巴開門』之禱開始。

sensitivity.note: Not excluded: record is built from published scholarly paraphrase only. Some Vodou/Santeria liturgical songs, veve drawings, and initiation knowledge ARE restricted (oungan/asogwe levels) and are not reproduced; see sensitivity_guidance.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the Fon narrative recorded by Herskovits (1938): Legba, youngest son of Mawu-Lisa, is set over the gates and the market road; he alone goes freely between the world of the gods and the world of men, carrying messages in both directions — and exploits the privilege, reporting each side's words to the other in altered form, until the old mother Mawu confirms his office: no one may come to the gods except through him. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the Fon narrative recorded by Herskovits (1938); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the Haitian ritual sequence described by Metraux (1959) and McCarthy Brown (1991): A Vodou service opens with the priye Legba at the poteau-mitan (center pole) and the drawn veve of the crossroads; the celebrant salutes Legba as old man, gatekeeper, opener of the way — 'pay for the gate, open the road' — before any other lwa may arrive. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the Haitian ritual sequence described by Metraux (1959) and McCarthy Brown (1991); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: No written canon; scholarly paraphrases (Herskovits 1938; Metraux 1959; McCarthy Brown 1991) are the published record

narrative.en:
Legba is the portmanteau god of the crossroads: a Fon (Dahomean) deity carried across the Middle Passage and enthroned in Haitian Vodou (and in cognate forms across the Afro-Atlantic world, from Brazilian Candomble Exu to Cuban Eleggua in Lucumi practice — cognate but distinct traditions).

THE FON ORIGIN: MESSENGER AND TRICKSTER. In the Dahomean narratives recorded by Herskovits in 1931 fieldwork, Mawu (the moon-mother, with Lisa her sun-twin) apportions the world among her children; Legba, the youngest and most wayward, receives no province — instead he is set over the gates, the roads, and the market crossroads, the in-between spaces. He alone travels freely between aye (the world of humans) and the world of the gods, and he makes the office his own: carrying messages up and down, he alters them for his own amusement — telling the gods that humans mock them, telling humans that the gods demand impossible fees — profiting in goats and palm wine from both sides of the gate. In the best-known episode, Legba's deception is discovered when Mawu (or in some tellings the hunter-god's households) sets a test; humiliated, Legba hides in a grass roof, and the fires of the gods' anger burn the grass house around him — but he survives through trickery, and the office stands: the mother confirms that nothing comes to the gods and nothing leaves them except through Legba. The narrative aitiologizes the ritual fact that all Fon and Vodou addresses begin with Legba's salutation.

THE HAITIAN THRONE: FIRST SERVED. In Haitian Vodou, Papa Legba (Legba Atibon) stands at the head of the lwa: the old man in rags with a straw hat, a crutch or machete, followed by a small white dog, smoking a pipe, guarding the crossroads at dawn. He is ritually first: no Vodou ceremony opens without the priye Legba, spoken at the poteau-mitan with the drawn veve (ritual flag/drawing) of the crossroads, saluting him as gatekeeper and 'opener of the way' — the lwa cannot descend to mount their servants until Legba has opened the gate between worlds. He is also the humblest of the great lwa — a beggar at the gate, poor and old — so that the highest threshold is kept by the least: a theological pole against pride, and a social image of the enslaved who kept their gods at the gates of the masters' world.

FUNCTIONS. Legba's narrative grounds Vodou ritual grammar (the priye and veve of the crossroads; the peristyle's center-pole as axis), the ethics of the marginal (gatekeeper as beggar), and the historical memory of the Middle Passage — the god of gates carried through the gate of slavery. His Fon stories aitiologize the market as cosmological meeting-place and the messenger's monopoly as both blessing and danger.

PROVENANCE NOTE. Key printed sources (Herskovits 1938) are colonial-era ethnography; contemporary community scholars (McCarthy Brown's partnership with Mama Lola/Alourdes, 1980s-90s; Gerdès Fleurant's ritual music studies) are preferred. Initiation-restricted liturgies (asogwe knowledge; secret society materials) are not represented here and are not reproduced.
narrative.zh: 豐族敘事（赫斯科維茨1931年田野）：瑪烏-麗莎分封諸子，幼子雷格巴無所封，得守門、路與市集路口，獨自在神人兩界間往來傳話；他篡改兩界之訊以取利，事發受辱，藏身草頂屋，神怒之火焚屋而不死；母神遂定其職：凡欲至神前者必經雷格巴。海地巫毒：雷格巴·阿蒂邦為羅亞之首，襤褸老者，草帽、杖、煙斗，隨一小白犬，守黎明之十字路口；每場儀式必先於中柱行『雷格巴之禱』、畫路口之韋韋旗，稱其『開路者』——羅亞降臨前必先請其開門。他同時是最卑微之神：守最高門檻者形同乞丐，釋奴隸神學之義。功能：巫毒儀式語法（開門禱與韋韋）、邊緣者倫理、以及穿越奴役之門的神話記憶。

functions: Ritual grammar: priye Legba opens every Vodou ceremony; veve of the crossroads
Cosmology of the in-between: market and crossroads as meeting of worlds
Ethics of the marginal: the highest gate kept by the humblest god
Middle Passage memory: the Fon gatekeeper enthroned in diaspora

variants.name: Fon Legba (Dahomey)
variants.text_tradition: Herskovits 1938 field recordings (1931, Abomey region), 2 vols.
variants.summary: Trickster-messenger of Mawu-Lisa, punished and confirmed in office; master of languages and the market; his narratives aitiologize the messenger monopoly.

variants.name: Haitian Legba Atibon
variants.summary: First-served lwa of the crossroads, saluted at dawn and at the poteau-mitan; merged iconographically with Catholic St. Lazarus/St. Peter under Code Noir Catholicism.

variants.name: Lucumi Eleggua / Candomble Exu
variants.text_tradition: Cuban Santeria and Brazilian Candomble (Yoruba-derived, distinct from Fon Legba)
variants.summary: Cognate crossroads tricksters of the Yoruba diaspora (Eshu/Eleggua; Exu), owner of roads and messenger of the orishas — structurally parallel to Legba but with separate Yoruba genealogy; do not conflate.

texts.sensitivity_guidance: Vodou is a living religion: initiation-level liturgies (asogwe knowledge), secret society materials, and some veve and song cycles are restricted and are NOT reproduced. This record paraphrases published scholarly sources only; prefer community-collaborative scholarship (McCarthy Brown; Fleurant); colonial-era collections (Herskovits) are flagged, not quoted verbatim. Do not photograph or publish ceremony images without the oungan/manbo's consent.
